web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: “Our year-to-date performance and customer demand give us confidence to raise our 2026 outlook for the third time this year.” [3]
epigraph.author: Simon Edwards, Chief Financial Officer

web_blocks.text: The market is not valuing Bloom as a conventional equipment vendor. At the verified 12 November close of $201.93, the latest share-count snapshot implies approximately $59.7 billion of equity value. Adding $295 million of net debt-like obligations from the September 2026 balance sheet produces an enterprise-value estimate near $60.0 billion. Management’s October 22 release raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $4.4–$4.6 billion, a $4.5 billion midpoint. That is roughly 13.3 times guided revenue. The multiple is the price of believing that power scarcity, high-load data centers, manufacturing demand and factory scale will translate into years of exceptional growth and much higher cash margins—not a market price supported by today’s free-cash-flow yield. [2][3][34][38]

The recent operating acceleration is real but must be read with its conversion cost. Q3 2026 revenue was $1.236 billion, up 138.1% year over year, and the company reported $225.4 million of GAAP operating income for the quarter. For the first nine months, revenue was $3.052 billion, CFO $272.9 million and cash PP&E purchases $231.3 million. CFO less PP&E was only $41.6 million before $26.6 million invested in affiliates. That leaves a thin cash margin against the scale now embedded in the share price. In other words, investors are paying for a future cash engine while the current business is still financing working capital and capacity. [2][3]

web_blocks.caption: Bloom Energy year-end price-to-sales proxy versus current as-of metrics [1][4][26][27][28][29][30][31][38][42]
rows: 15.65x current P/S; 13.33x EV / FY2026 guide midpoint
web_blocks.takeaway: Historical figures are a deliberately labeled market-cap-to-sales proxy: year-end close × annual diluted weighted-average shares ÷ reported annual revenue. Weighted-average shares are not exact year-end shares, so this is a range-setting approximation, not a clean annual EV/Sales series. Current P/S uses the latest displayed TTM sales and Nov 12 close; the forward EV/Sales denominator is management guidance.

web_blocks.text: This history explains why “the old multiple” is not a simple anchor. Bloom reported losses in several of the years shown, so a P/E band would be unstable or meaningless. The rough P/S proxy ranged from about 2.4x to 10.3x at fiscal year-end between 2021 and 2025, then rose to approximately 15.7x on trailing sales by the Nov 12 close. The 2025 jump already reflected AI-power expectations; the 2026 price now requires that demand to become accepted installations and recurring cash. The current valuation is above even the high end of this approximate five-year band, while the company still has negative net income for FY2025 and only modest cash after plant spending in 2026 year to date. [1][2][3][4][26][27][28][29][30][31][38][42]

web_blocks.caption: BE against three listed power and data-center infrastructure comparables — Nov 12 close aligned snapshot [34][35][36][37][38][39][40][41]
web_blocks.takeaway: These are adjacent operating comparables, not pure-play SOFC peers: Cummins adds engines and distributed power, GE Vernova sells generation/grid equipment, and Vertiv supplies data-center power and cooling. Values are a same-cutoff screen, not like-for-like forecasts. BE is materially more expensive on sales and trailing earnings, while the peers carry different mixes, growth, balance sheets and cyclicality.

web_blocks.text: The peer comparison makes the premium visible without pretending that one multiple settles the question. The as-of-aligned snapshot places BE near 15.7x trailing sales and about 125.6x trailing earnings; the same table shows Cummins around 19x earnings and 4.7x book, GE Vernova around 21.5x earnings, and Vertiv around 39x earnings. On enterprise value to sales, the adjacent-company screen is approximately 1.9x for CMI, 4.6x for GEV and 6.1x for VRT versus 15.8x for BE. These differences are not proof that Bloom is mispriced: Vertiv, Cummins and GE Vernova have distinct margin, service and product structures. They do show that Bloom’s price assumes a much larger future cash contribution from each current revenue dollar. [34][35][36][37][38][39][40][41]

The reverse DCF asks what must happen for the enterprise value to make sense. The model starts at $4.5 billion of FY2026 guided revenue and a 1.36% starting FCF margin, the first-nine-month CFO-minus-PP&E ratio. It projects ten years, ramps the FCF margin linearly to a scenario terminal margin, discounts yearly cash flows, applies a 3.0% or 2.5% terminal-growth assumption, subtracts $295 million of disclosed net debt-like obligations, and divides scenario equity value by 324.289 million Q3 diluted weighted-average shares. The 10% base discount rate is an analyst hurdle, not a market-implied WACC or management forecast. The calculation is deterministic; the forecast assumptions are judgment. [1][2][3]

web_blocks.caption: Ten-year DCF sensitivity and probability-weighted per-share outcomes (USD) [1][2][3]
web_blocks.takeaway: The base value is below both the Nov 12 close and the technical support band. Terminal value contributes about 76% of base-case DCF value and 85% in the bull case; the apparent precision is therefore much lower than the cents shown. A 15% terminal FCF margin, 10% discount rate and 3% terminal growth would require roughly 28.7% annual revenue growth for ten years to support today’s enterprise value.

web_blocks.text: The bull case is intentionally generous: it assumes 30% annual sales growth for a decade, an 18% terminal FCF margin and an 8% discount rate. That outcome can exceed today’s price, but it requires both growth and durable cash conversion that Bloom has not yet demonstrated through a full cycle. The bear case is not a liquidation case; it still assumes 12% annual growth and a 6% terminal FCF margin, yet its value is only about $13.50 per diluted share because the starting enterprise value is so large. The probability-weighted value is about $97.30, roughly 52% below the $201.93 cutoff price. Changing the margins and discount rates changes that conclusion, which is precisely why the premium is not an automatic buy signal. [1][2][3]

The price therefore reflects a contest between a genuine secular bottleneck and a demanding conversion schedule. Bloom can win when customers cannot secure timely grid power, when fuel and tariff economics work, and when financiers fund deployments. Yet a large customer framework is not current revenue, revenue is not cash, and gross profit on equipment does not capture the future cost of field service, installation guarantees and plant capacity. My independent judgment is that investors are paying for a favorable decade before Bloom has established a decade-long record of cash returns. The platform deserves a place in the industry conversation; the current price does not provide a base-case margin of safety. [1][2][3][18][19][20][21]

book_paragraphs: Let us separate the good business story from the price you are asked to pay. At the Nov 12 close of $201.93, Bloom’s equity value was about $59.7 billion using the latest share-count snapshot. The September balance sheet adds about $295 million of net debt-like obligations after cash, lease and financing liabilities. That produces an enterprise value near $60 billion. Management’s $4.4–$4.6 billion revenue guidance for 2026 gives a $4.5 billion midpoint, so the market is valuing the company at about 13.3 times this year’s guided sales. You are not paying for today’s cash yield; you are paying for a future business that must grow into this value. [2][3][34][38]

Look at the actual financial bridge before accepting that future. Q3 revenue was $1.236 billion, while first-nine-month CFO was $272.9 million and PP&E purchases were $231.3 million. That leaves roughly $41.6 million before affiliate investment, a narrow margin on more than $3 billion of sales. The demand step-up can be valuable and the cash conversion can still be unfinished. You should ask which quarter’s cash flow funds the next factory and how much working capital a new installation needs before customer acceptance. [2][3]

The five-year price-to-sales proxy adds historical context. It was about 3.9 times at year-end 2021, 3.0 times in 2022, 2.4 times in 2023, 3.4 times in 2024 and 10.3 times in 2025. The current trailing P/S is about 15.7 times. These historical points use year-end closes and annual diluted weighted-average shares, not exact shares outstanding on each final trading day; they are a rough capitalization-to-sales series. P/E is a weak historical yardstick because reported earnings were negative in several periods. Still, the range tells you that the market’s expectations have expanded faster than the long-run accounting record. [1][4][26][27][28][29][30][31][38][42]

Now compare the adjacent businesses. Cummins makes engines and power systems, GE Vernova serves generation and grid markets, and Vertiv sells data-center power and cooling equipment. The aligned snapshot shows their very different valuation and margin profiles beside Bloom. The right question is not which ticker has the lowest multiple. It is what earns Bloom a premium: the scarcity of fast power, solid-oxide efficiency, modular deployment and a growing service base. That premium is justified only if the firm converts customer interest into installed equipment, dependable service and returns on the factory capital. [34][35][36][37][38][39][40][41]

The reverse DCF makes the expectation concrete. We begin with $4.5 billion of FY2026 revenue guidance and a 1.36% starting free-cash-flow margin, based on the first nine months’ cash from operations less PP&E purchases divided by revenue. We then project ten years of sales, ramp FCF margins, discount them and calculate a terminal value. The 10% base discount rate is our underwriting assumption, not a market-derived WACC. We subtract debt-like obligations net of cash and divide by 324.289 million diluted weighted-average shares. You should notice what comes from a filing and what comes from us: revenue, CFO, capex and diluted shares are disclosed; future growth, FCF margin and discount rates are scenarios. [1][2][3]

The bear case assumes 12% annual revenue growth and a 6% terminal FCF margin, yet it produces about $13.50 a share. The base assumes 20% growth and a 12% terminal margin, yielding about $75.98. The bull assumes 30% annual growth, 18% terminal FCF margin and an 8% discount rate, yielding about $384.71. At 40%, 45% and 15% weights, expected value is about $97.30 per diluted share. That is not an official target; it is a transparent way to show how much the current quote depends on the bull path. [1][2][3]

A reverse calculation asks how much growth the current enterprise value needs. Under a 15% terminal FCF margin, a 10% discount rate and 3% perpetual growth, revenue must compound about 28.7% annually for ten years from the $4.5 billion starting point. Bloom grew rapidly from a small base and management now expects a one-year step-change, but sustaining nearly 29% through a much larger base while converting to cash is a separate challenge. The base DCF’s terminal value is about 76% of total value, so a small change in long-run assumptions moves the answer materially. [1][2][3][4]

This is why I would not let a powerful story substitute for valuation discipline. There is a real customer problem and credible evidence of deployment. But financing frameworks, announcements and megawatt totals are not the same as collected cash or returns on invested capital. My conclusion is that Bloom may become a much larger power platform, but the current quote discounts a favorable decade before the filings prove that the new scale can earn attractive cash returns. You can admire the technology and still decline the stock at this price. [1][2][3][18][19][20][21]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: You have two separate questions in front of you: can Bloom win a meaningful market, and can the cash it earns justify today’s enterprise value? The evidence gives a credible yes to the first and no clear yes to the second. A disciplined investor can respect the operating opportunity without paying any price for it.
